title: Periodic Table and Periodicity in Properties
tagline: Modern Periodic Law, the periodic table, and trends in atomic and ionic radii, valency, ionisation enthalpy, electron-gain enthalpy, electronegativity and metallic character.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Chemistry syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Chemistry registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: The periodic table is one of the most useful organising ideas in chemistry. When elements are arranged by atomic number, their physical and chemical properties show a repeating pattern. This chapter explains why that happens, and then uses the idea to understand trends in atomic size, ionic size, valency, ionisation enthalpy, electron-gain enthalpy, electronegativity and metallic character. The goal is not to memorise arrows, but to understand the reasons behind the trends so that exceptions and comparisons can be explained rather than guessed.

learningOutcomes: Explain why elements show periodic trends.
Compare atomic and ionic sizes across periods and groups.
Define ionisation enthalpy and electron-gain enthalpy.
Define electronegativity and distinguish it from electron-gain enthalpy.
Explain metallic and non-metallic character trends.
Name elements with atomic numbers above 100 using IUPAC nomenclature.

learn.title: Modern Periodic Law and the periodic table

blocks.text: The Modern Periodic Law says that the physical and chemical properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers. That is why the modern table is arranged by atomic number, not by atomic mass. As the atomic number increases, the electronic configuration repeats in a regular way, and that repetition is what gives rise to periodicity. The table is divided into periods, groups and blocks, and an element’s position reflects its valence-shell configuration.

items: Modern Periodic Law: properties are a periodic function of atomic number.
Atomic number determines the electronic configuration.
Periods are horizontal rows; groups are vertical columns.
An element’s position is linked to its valence electrons.
The table has s, p, d and f blocks.

items.text: Elements in the same group have similar valence-shell configurations, which is why they often show similar chemical properties. A group is vertical and a period is horizontal.
items.note: Periodicity is not magic; it comes from the repetition of similar outer electronic arrangements.

blocks.text: Atomic radius is a measure of the size of an atom, and ionic radius is a measure of the size of an ion. Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases because the outer electrons are added to the same shell while the nuclear charge increases. Down a group, atomic radius generally increases because extra shells are added. When an atom becomes a cation, it is usually smaller than the parent atom, and when it becomes an anion, it is usually larger.

items: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period.
Atomic radius generally increases down a group.
Cations are generally smaller than the parent atom.
Anions are generally larger than the parent atom.
Compare radii using the same type of radius where possible.

items.text: In Period 3, sodium is larger than chlorine, because the outer electrons are in the same shell but chlorine has a greater effective nuclear attraction pulling them in.
items.note: Across a period, the important change is the increasing attraction on the same outermost shell.

blocks.text: Ionisation enthalpy is the enthalpy change when an electron is removed from a gaseous atom or ion. The first ionisation enthalpy refers to removing the first electron from a neutral gaseous atom. Ionisation enthalpy is always positive, because energy is required to overcome the attraction between the nucleus and the electron. It generally increases across a period and decreases down a group, for reasons similar to those in atomic size trends.

items: Ionisation enthalpy is the energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom or ion.
The first ionisation enthalpy is for a neutral gaseous atom.
Ionisation enthalpy is endothermic.
It generally increases across a period.
It generally decreases down a group.

items.text: It is harder to remove an electron from a small atom with a strong nuclear attraction than from a larger one with electron shielding, so the trend can be understood in terms of size and effective nuclear charge.
items.note: The sign is important: ionisation enthalpy is positive because energy must be supplied.

blocks.text: Electron-gain enthalpy is the enthalpy change when a gaseous atom accepts an electron. It can be negative or positive, depending on the element. A negative value means energy is released when the electron is added, which is more favourable. A positive value means energy must be supplied. Trends are not as simple as for ionisation enthalpy, and the sign convention must be handled carefully. Electron-gain enthalpy is also not the same as electronegativity.

items: Electron-gain enthalpy is the enthalpy change on adding an electron to a gaseous atom.
It can be negative or positive.
A more negative value is usually more favourable.
It is not the same as electronegativity.
Trends require caution because of exceptions and sign conventions.

items.text: Chlorine often shows a very favourable electron-gain enthalpy because adding an electron helps it approach a stable configuration; this is one reason chlorine is strongly reactive in many situations.
items.note: Electron-gain enthalpy describes a gaseous atom gaining an electron; it is a different idea from the electronegativity used in bonds.

blocks.text: Electronegativity is a measure of the tendency of an atom in a bond to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself. It is a relative concept, not an exact energy value like ionisation enthalpy or electron-gain enthalpy. Electronegativity generally increases across a period and decreases down a group. The idea is useful because it helps predict bond polarity and the nature of the bonding between two atoms.

items: Electronegativity is the tendency to attract shared electrons in a bond.
It is a relative measure, not a direct energy change.
It generally increases across a period.
It generally decreases down a group.
A large difference in electronegativity usually suggests stronger bond polarity.

items.text: Fluorine is one of the most electronegative elements, so in a bond between fluorine and hydrogen, the shared electrons are drawn more toward fluorine.
items.note: Electronegativity is used for atoms in compounds, not for isolated gaseous atoms in the same way as electron-gain enthalpy.

blocks.text: Metallic character is linked to the tendency to lose electrons, while non-metallic character is linked to the tendency to gain or attract electrons. Across a period, metallic character generally decreases and non-metallic character increases. Down a group, metallic character generally increases. These trends are useful for predicting chemical behaviour, because the type of element affects the kinds of compounds it forms.

items: Metallic character is linked to losing electrons.
Non-metallic character is linked to gaining or attracting electrons.
Metallic character generally decreases across a period.
Metallic character generally increases down a group.
These trends connect to ionisation enthalpy and electronegativity.

items.text: Sodium is strongly metallic, while chlorine is strongly non-metallic; their positions in the periodic table reflect these opposite tendencies.
items.note: Metallic and non-metallic character are opposite ends of a general trend, not rigid categories for every element.

blocks.text: For elements with very high atomic numbers, systematic IUPAC names are used until the element is given an official name. These names are built from numerical roots for each digit of the atomic number, followed by the ending -ium. Learning the roots makes it possible to write the systematic name of a superheavy element from its atomic number.

items: IUPAC systematic names are used for unnamed elements above 100.
The name is built from numerical roots.
The ending is -ium.
This avoids confusion before an official name is adopted.

items.text: An element with atomic number 118 has the systematic name built from the digits 1-1-8, giving the name based on the corresponding numerical roots and the ending -ium.
items.note: The point is to know the method, not just one example; once you know the roots, you can build the name for any high atomic number.

keyPoints: Modern Periodic Law: properties are a periodic function of atomic number.
Atomic radius generally decreases across a period and increases down a group.
Cations are generally smaller and anions larger than the parent atom.
Ionisation enthalpy is the energy for removing an electron; it is always positive.
Electron-gain enthalpy is the enthalpy change on adding an electron; it can be negative or positive.
Electronegativity is a relative measure of electron attraction in a bond.
Metallic character generally decreases across a period and increases down a group.
examFocus: When comparing trends, state the direction clearly and give the reason, such as increasing nuclear attraction or added shells, rather than only writing an arrow.
Do not treat electron-gain enthalpy and electronegativity as the same thing; they are related but different ideas.

vocabulary.meaning: The statement that properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.
A measure of the size of an atom.
The enthalpy change when an electron is removed from a gaseous atom or ion.
The enthalpy change when a gaseous atom accepts an electron.
The tendency of an atom in a bond to attract shared electrons.
The tendency of an element to behave as a metal, often related to ease of losing electrons.

questions.prompt: The Modern Periodic Law states that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their:
questions.explanation: The Modern Periodic Law is based on atomic number, not atomic mass.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking the modern table still follows Mendeleev’s atomic-mass ordering.

questions.prompt: Across a period, atomic radius generally:
options: First increases then decreases in every case
questions.explanation: Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases because effective nuclear attraction increases for the same outermost shell.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming atomic size always increases with atomic number.

questions.prompt: Why is ionisation enthalpy always positive?
questions.answer: Because energy must be supplied to remove an electron from an atom or ion against nuclear attraction.
questions.explanation: Ionisation enthalpy is an endothermic process.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking it can be negative because atoms are stable.

questions.answer: Electronegativity is a relative tendency of an atom in a bond to attract shared electrons. Electron-gain enthalpy is an enthalpy change when a gaseous atom accepts an electron.
questions.explanation: They are related, but electronegativity is a bonding concept while electron-gain enthalpy is an energetic one.

questions.prompt: Explain why sodium is larger than chlorine and why Na+ is smaller than Na.
questions.answer: Sodium is larger than chlorine because both have outer electrons in the same period, but chlorine has a greater nuclear attraction pulling the electrons in. When sodium loses an electron to form Na+, it loses its outermost shell and the remaining electrons are held more strongly, so Na+ is much smaller than Na.
questions.explanation: The size change across a period and the size change on ion formation both come from changes in effective nuclear attraction and the number of occupied shells.
questions.commonMistake: Saying Na+ is larger because it is a positive ion, or giving the trend without explaining the reason.
